Ken Dryden is a Canadian goaltender and Harvard graduate who rose to dominance in the nineteen seventies with the Montreal Canadiens, winning six Stanley Cups in an eight-year career marked by intellectual sophistication and exceptional play.

He won six Stanley Cups with the Montreal Canadiens in nineteen seventy-one, nineteen seventy-three, nineteen seventy-six, nineteen seventy-seven, nineteen seventy-eight, and nineteen seventy-nine in just eight seasons, more cups per season than nearly any goaltender in history. Dryden won the Conn Smythe Trophy for playoff MVP four times, appearing in six straight Finals and becoming the greatest playoff performer of his era. He recorded a two point twenty-four goals-against average over three hundred ninety-seven games and a nine hundred twenty-two save percentage, exceptionally low for the high-scoring nineteen seventies.

He won the Vezina Trophy for best goaltender five times in six years from nineteen seventy-three to nineteen seventy-nine, establishing goaltending dominance during the Canadiens dynasty. Dryden was unique among hockey players for his intellectual approach to the game. He wrote extensively about hockey philosophy and later became a broadcaster and author. He pioneered the stand-up goaltending style with excellent positioning and rebound control, influencing generations of net minders. He attended Cornell University on an academic scholarship and remained a Rhodes Scholar finalist, embodying the rare athlete-intellectual.
